stated_availability: Three distinct statements, descriptive only (not mapped to L1-L6). (1) Data availability statement (p. 8): "Supplementary Information to this article can be found online at https://zenodo.org/records/10801706." (2) Methods section 2.2 (p. 3): "Dedicated R code and complete data tables are reported in Supplementary Information S2 and S3. All analyses were performed in the open-source R programming environment (v.4.2.2; R Core Team, 2021), using the Quanteda package (Benoit et al., 2018). All code and data are available here: https://zenodo.org/records/10623550." (3) Appendix A: "Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2024.105969." Section 2 also cites "a total of 483 objects (Supplementary Information S1)". Article licence stated on p. 1: "This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)." Note: two different Zenodo record identifiers (10623550 and 10801706) are cited for the accompanying materials; neither is printed as a DOI string. Funding: "No funding sources were involved in this article." No ORCIDs printed; CRediT statement present but assigns no Software role.

F1.evidence: Deposit identified by Zenodo record accessions: "All code and data are available here: https://zenodo.org/records/10623550" (Methods 2.2, p. 3) and "Supplementary Information to this article can be found online at https://zenodo.org/records/10801706" (Data availability statement, p. 8). Zenodo record IDs are globally unique repository accessions in a DataCite-registered registry, satisfying the instrument's F1 enumeration ("DOI, IGSN, SWHID, accession"). Caveat recorded: the paper prints record URLs, not explicit DOI strings (e.g. no 10.5281/zenodo.* form), and cites two different record numbers for the same materials.

F2.evidence: Materials deposited in Zenodo, which generates structured DataCite metadata (creators, title, description, resource type, publication year) for every record. The paper further evidences descriptive richness of the deposited data itself: "These data consist of numerous categorical variables corresponding to the characteristics of each ornamented object and associated metadata such as location, quality of contextual information, and original source" (p. 2).

F3.evidence: Zenodo/DataCite records carry the record identifier within their own metadata payload as a matter of platform design, so the metadata describing the deposit explicitly includes the identifier by which the deposit is retrieved (https://zenodo.org/records/10623550, https://zenodo.org/records/10801706).

F4.evidence: Deposited in Zenodo, named explicitly in the instrument as a qualifying searchable registry ("F4: Resource indexed in searchable registry (Zenodo, CRAN, DataCite)"). Paper cites two Zenodo records (10623550, 10801706).

A1.evidence: Retrievable via HTTPS from Zenodo: "All code and data are available here: https://zenodo.org/records/10623550" (p. 3). Assessed against the full research dataset per the completeness rule: coverage_category is "substantial" (75%; 3 of 4 enumerated datasets at Tier 0), and record-weighted coverage is approximately 100% because all 483 analysed objects sit in the deposited digitised dataset ("With a total of 483 objects (Supplementary Information S1)", p. 2). Since coverage is neither "minimal" nor "partial", A1 is not forced to 0; a majority of the research data is retrievable by standard protocol.

A1_1.evidence: Access is by HTTPS to a public Zenodo record with no login, subscription, or proprietary client required. The analysis environment is likewise open: "All analyses were performed in the open-source R programming environment (v.4.2.2; R Core Team, 2021), using the Quanteda package (Benoit et al., 2018)" (p. 3).

A1_2.evidence: No access restriction is required for this material (motif codings transcribed from a published catalogue of museum-held Mesolithic portable art; no human subjects, Indigenous, or otherwise sensitive data), and none is imposed. The retrieval protocol (HTTPS via Zenodo) supports authentication/authorisation procedures where they are necessary, so the sub-principle is met; there is no unjustified closure.

A2.evidence: Deposited in Zenodo, a repository with an institutional commitment to metadata persistence (DataCite-registered metadata and tombstone records survive withdrawal of the files). The instrument credits exactly this case ("Repository committed to metadata persistence (Zenodo, DANS, institutional commitment)").

I1.evidence: Data are structured tabular/categorical by construction and deposited alongside executable R code: "Dedicated R code and complete data tables are reported in Supplementary Information S2 and S3" (p. 3); "Plonka's (2003, pp. 315-325) own motif classification scheme ... was transcribed as binary data in the form of presence/absence coding of motif types (named A1, A2, etc.) on each individual artefact" (p. 2). For the deposited R/quanteda pipeline to run, the data must be in a machine-parseable representation. Inference limit noted: the paper states no file formats, and the deposit was not inspected (paper is the sole source).

I2.evidence: No FAIR vocabulary is used. The motif taxonomy is Plonka's own idiosyncratic scheme from a print monograph ("named A1, A2, etc.", p. 2), chronological units are conventional culture-historical labels ("Maglemose (~11,000-8400 BP), Kongemose (~8400-7400 BP), and Erteboelle (~7400-5950 BP)", p. 2) with no PeriodO URIs, and artefact classes (axe, shaft, pendant, etc., Fig. 2) are ad hoc. No Getty AAT, CIDOC-CRM, PeriodO, Pleiades, or ARIADNEplus vocabulary is cited. The authors acknowledge the taxonomic looseness: "We have not, in our analysis, tested for inter-coder consistency (such as in Dutkiewicz et al., 2020), nor have we explored the effects of variable classifications of related motifs" (p. 7).

I3.evidence: No qualified, typed PID references from the data artefact are evidenced. The upstream source is cited only as a bibliographic reference with no PID: "Plonka, T., 2003. The portable art of mesolithic europe, acta universitatis wratislaviensis. Wydawn. Uniw. Wroclawskiego, Wroclaw" (reference list, p. 9) - no DOI. No "isDerivedFrom"/"isSupplementTo" relationship assertions are stated in the paper, and the two cited Zenodo records are not linked to each other or to the article DOI by any stated typed relation.

R1.evidence: Plurality of relevant attributes explicitly documented: "These data consist of numerous categorical variables corresponding to the characteristics of each ornamented object and associated metadata such as location, quality of contextual information, and original source" (p. 2); "We do include pertinent metadata such as artefact classes, chronology, and spatial distribution that can be drawn upon in substantiating claims for semiotic significance" (p. 7). Table 3 exemplifies the per-object attribute set (site, region, artefact type, motifs, source figure in Plonka 2003).

R1_1.evidence: Explicit, standard, URL-linked licence covering the article and its supplementary information, where S1-S3 are reported: "This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)" (p. 1), with Appendix A directing supplementary data to the article DOI ("Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2024.105969"). Caveat recorded: the paper states no separate licence for the Zenodo deposits themselves.

R1_2.evidence: Detailed provenance chain documented in Methods: source ("the comprehensive catalogue of Mesolithic ornamentation compiled by Plonka (2003)"), extraction ("From this analogue compilation, the South Scandinavian data were manually extracted and digitised"), coding ("transcribed as binary data in the form of presence/absence coding"), transformation ("transformed from presence/absence coding into a sentence-imitating structure"), parameters ("the k value for all generated skipgrams is thus set to 13", plus the printed expected-frequency and PMI formulae), and software versions (R v.4.2.2, quanteda). "Original source" is additionally retained as a per-object variable.

R1_3.evidence: No domain-relevant community standard is met. Deposit is to a general-purpose repository (Zenodo), not an archaeological domain repository (tDAR, Open Context, ARIADNEplus), and no domain metadata schema (Dublin Core profile, CIDOC-CRM, ARIADNE) is stated. The paper itself contrasts its approach with the emerging open standard it did not adopt: "Open-source databases of prehistoric art are emerging (e.g., Dutkiewicz et al., 2020)" (p. 2, referring to SignBase), and the analysis rests instead on "this analogue compilation".

F1.evidence: Code shares the Zenodo record accession with the data: "All code and data are available here: https://zenodo.org/records/10623550" (Methods 2.2, p. 3). A Zenodo record ID is a globally unique repository accession per the instrument's F1 enumeration. Caveat: no DOI string, SWHID, or CRAN/JOSS identifier is printed for the code, and a second record (10801706) is cited in the Data availability statement.

F2.evidence: Code deposited in Zenodo, which auto-generates structured DataCite metadata (creators, title, description, resource type, year). The paper supplies the code's identity and purpose: "Dedicated R code and complete data tables are reported in Supplementary Information S2 and S3" (p. 3). No CodeMeta.json or CITATION.cff is evidenced, but the sub-principle's stated fields (authors, title, keywords, description) are met by the Zenodo record.

F3.evidence: The Zenodo/DataCite metadata record for the deposit carries its own record identifier by platform design, so the metadata describing the code explicitly includes the identifier used to retrieve it (https://zenodo.org/records/10623550).

F4.evidence: Archived in Zenodo, explicitly named in the instrument as a qualifying searchable registry ("F4: Resource indexed in searchable registry (Zenodo, CRAN, DataCite)"). Not a live-repository-only (GitHub) deposit, so the persistence penalty does not apply.

A1.evidence: Code retrievable by standard protocol (HTTPS) from the cited Zenodo record: "All code and data are available here: https://zenodo.org/records/10623550" (p. 3), reinforced by "Dedicated R code ... reported in Supplementary Information S2". No email request or gatekeeping is interposed.

A1_1.evidence: HTTPS retrieval from a public Zenodo record with no login or paid subscription, and the code targets an open runtime: "All analyses were performed in the open-source R programming environment (v.4.2.2; R Core Team, 2021), using the Quanteda package (Benoit et al., 2018)" (p. 3). The Conclusion also frames this deliberately: "approaches such as the skipgram methodology are implemented in open-source software solutions that promote transparency and replicability" (pp. 7-8).

A1_2.evidence: No access restriction is warranted or imposed for this analysis code, and the retrieval protocol (HTTPS via Zenodo) supports authentication/authorisation procedures where necessary. There is no unjustified closure and no proprietary or licence-gated dependency.

A2.evidence: Zenodo archival means the deposit's DataCite metadata persists independently of file availability (tombstone records), satisfying the instrument's metadata-persistence criterion for a repository with institutional commitment.

I1.evidence: Code is written in R, a formal, open, broadly applicable and widely implemented language: "All analyses were performed in the open-source R programming environment (v.4.2.2; R Core Team, 2021), using the Quanteda package (Benoit et al., 2018)" (p. 3). Source is shared as code ("Dedicated R code"), not as compiled binaries or prose description.

I2.evidence: No FAIR vocabulary or software metadata ontology is evidenced for the code artefact - no CodeMeta.json, no CITATION.cff, no schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode assertion, no controlled vocabulary for variables or motif codes. Identifiers used within the analysis are the paper's own ad hoc motif labels ("named A1, A2, etc.", p. 2).

I3.evidence: No qualified, typed references from the code artefact are evidenced. Dependencies are named only in the paper's prose and reference list (R Core Team 2021, listed without a DOI; quanteda cited as Benoit et al. 2018 with https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.00774), not as machine-actionable typed relations from the deposit. No renv.lock, DESCRIPTION, or dependency manifest with PIDs is mentioned, and no "isSupplementTo" link to the article DOI is asserted.

R1.evidence: The code is accompanied by a plurality of reuse-relevant attributes: pinned runtime and package ("the open-source R programming environment (v.4.2.2 ...), using the Quanteda package"), the full analytical specification ("the k value for all generated skipgrams is thus set to 13", p. 3, plus the printed expected-frequency and PMI equations), the output levels produced ("The case study presents results at the level of 2-, 3-, and 4-grams"), and co-deposit with the data it operates on. Caveat: no README, installation instructions, or test suite is evidenced from the paper.

R1_1.evidence: The code is reported as Supplementary Information S2 to an article carrying an explicit, standard, URL-linked licence: "This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)" (p. 1), with Appendix A pointing supplementary data to the article DOI. Caveat recorded: no separate software licence (MIT, GPL, Apache-2.0) is stated for the Zenodo deposit, and CC BY is a content rather than software licence.

R1_2.evidence: Execution provenance documented: software and version (R v.4.2.2), package (quanteda, with citation), algorithm parameters (k = 13; expected frequency and PMI formulae printed on p. 3), and the full transformation sequence from Plonka's catalogue through digitisation, binary coding, sentence-imitating strings, skipgram generation, and PMI calculation. Authorship provenance via CRediT (p. 8): "Lasse Lukas Platz Herskind: ... Methodology, Investigation, Formal analysis, Data curation ...". The computation is deterministic, so absence of a random seed is not a provenance gap.

R1_3.evidence: No research-software community standard is met: no CodeMeta.json, CITATION.cff, CRAN/rOpenSci packaging, JOSS submission, containerisation (Dockerfile), or dependency lockfile is evidenced; the artefact is described only as "Dedicated R code" (p. 3). Notably the CRediT statement (p. 8) assigns no Software role to either author, and no software-citation standard is applied to the deposit.
